title: At home — there is, there isn't
goal: Name rooms and furniture, say that something is or isn't somewhere, and make nouns plural.
bekal: use هست and نیست to say that something exists
put things in their place with رویِ، زیرِ، تویِ، پشتِ، جلویِ، کنارِ
form plurals with ـها and know when you don't need one

dialogs.title: گفتگو — بازدید از آپارتمان
dialogs.intro: Budi is looking for a place to live. A landlady, Mrs. Ahmadi, shows him a small apartment in north Tehran.

lines.speaker: خانمِ احمدی:
lines.text: بفرمایید تو. این آپارتمانِ ما است.
lines.baca: befarmâyid tu. in âpârtemân-e mâ ast.
lines.id: Please come in. This is our apartment.
lines.literal: please inside. this apartment-of we is.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: چه روشن است! چند اتاق دارد؟
lines.baca: che rowshan ast! chand otâgh dârad?
lines.id: It's so bright! How many rooms does it have?
lines.literal: what bright is! how-many room has-it?

lines.speaker: خانمِ احمدی:
lines.text: دو اتاقِ خواب، یک نشیمن، آشپزخانه و حمام.
lines.baca: do otâgh-e khâb, yek neshiman, âshpazkhâne va hammâm.
lines.id: Two bedrooms, a living room, a kitchen, and a bathroom.
lines.literal: two room-of sleep, one living-room, kitchen and bathroom.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.id: Is there a fridge in the kitchen?

lines.speaker: خانمِ احمدی:
lines.text: بله، یخچال و اجاق هست. ولی ماشینِ لباسشویی نیست.
lines.baca: bale, yakhchâl va ojâgh hast. vali mâshin-e lebâsshuyi nist.
lines.id: Yes, there's a fridge and a stove. But there's no washing machine.
lines.literal: yes, fridge and stove there-is. but machine-of wash-clothes there-isn't.

lines.speaker: خانمِ احمدی:
lines.text: در اتاقِ اول یک تخت هست. کمد هم کنارِ پنجره است.
lines.baca: dar otâgh-e avval yek takht hast. komod ham kenâr-e panjere ast.
lines.id: There's a bed in the first room. And the wardrobe is next to the window.
lines.literal: in room-of first one bed there-is. wardrobe also side-of window is.

lines.speaker: خانمِ احمدی:
lines.text: شوفاژ است. زمستان‌ها اینجا خیلی گرم می‌شود.
lines.baca: shufâzh ast. zemestânhâ injâ kheyli garm mishavad.
lines.id: That's the radiator. In winter it gets very warm here.
lines.literal: radiator is. winters here very warm becomes.

lines.speaker: خانمِ احمدی:
lines.text: خیلی خوب. طبقهٔ پایین یک خانوادهٔ کوچک است.
lines.baca: kheyli khub. tabaghe-ye pâyin yek khânevâde-ye kuchak ast.
lines.id: Very nice. There's a small family on the floor below.
lines.literal: very good. floor-of below one family-of small is.

lines.speaker: خانمِ احمدی:
lines.text: متأسفانه نیست. ولی فقط سه طبقه است.
lines.baca: mota'assefâne nist. vali faghat se tabaghe ast.
lines.id: Unfortunately not. But it's only three floors.
lines.literal: unfortunately there-isn't. but only three floor is.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: خوب است. خیلی ممنون از وقتتان.
lines.baca: khub ast. kheyli mamnun az vaghtetân.
lines.id: Good. Thank you very much for your time.
lines.literal: good is. very grateful from time-your.

lines.speaker: خانمِ احمدی:
lines.id: You're welcome. Make yourself at home.

notes: **Both have the same negative: نیست.** یخچال نیست can mean "it isn't a fridge" or "there is no fridge", and context decides. This is the only place where the two meanings overlap.

**"No problem" is اشکالی ندارد.** Learn it whole, along with its siblings عیبی ندارد (*eybi nadârad*) and مشکلی نیست (*moshkeli nist*). All three mean the same and are equally common. Notice that all three use the little ـی ending you learned in unit 3.
**Look at همسایه‌ها چطورند؟** and the ending ـند on چطور: even a question word takes the plural "be" ending, because the question is about several people. Persian is very tidy about this.

**Three French words, آسانسور، شوفاژ، کمد,** have settled into Persian (*ascenseur*, *chauffage*, *commode* — the last one is in English too). As mentioned in unit 2: if you don't know the name of a modern object, the French word is often a good guess.

**"This is your own home": خانهٔ خودتان است.** It isn't a real offer; it's تعارف, a courtesy phrase hosts say to guests. Don't respond by moving your suitcases in. Just answer ممنون or لطف دارید. The details come in unit 15.

**Spoken forms in this dialogue:** بفرمایید تو (*befarmâyin tu*), یخچال هست؟ (*yakhchâl hast?* — unchanged), نیست (*nist* — unchanged), همسایه‌ها چطورن؟ (*hamsâyehâ chetowran?*). Notice that هست and نیست are among the words that **don't change** between written and spoken Persian — a small gift.

grammars.title: هست / نیست — there is, there isn't
body: To say that something exists or is available somewhere, Persian uses هست, and for the opposite نیست. The sentence puts **the place first**, the thing in the middle, and هست at the end.

head: Persian
Say it
Meaning
rows: There is a table in the room.
There is a book on the table.

after: To ask a question, nothing changes but your tone of voice: آسانسور هست؟ ("is there an elevator?").
**The word هست can also be an emphatic "is".** او اینجا هست ("he really is here") sounds firmer than او اینجا است. The difference is subtle and won't trip you up at A1.
⚠️ Don't confuse نیست ("there isn't / is not") with ندارد ("he/she doesn't have"). یخچال نیست = "there is no fridge" (in that place). یخچال ندارم = "I don't have a fridge".

grammars.title: Prepositions of place — they all use ezafe
body: Almost all Persian prepositions of place are really **nouns** ("top", "bottom", "inside") linked to the next word with ezafe. That's why they all end in -e.

head: Persian
Say it
Meaning
Example
Meaning
rows: in the middle of the room
at the top of the mountain

after: **The exception is در** ("in"): it is a true preposition and takes **no** ezafe — در خانه ("at home"), در تهران ("in Tehran"). In conversation it is almost always replaced by **تو**: تویِ خانه (*tu-ye khune*).
When the preposition stands alone with no noun after it, the ezafe disappears: کتاب رویِ میز است ("the book is on the table") but کتاب بالا است ("the book is up there").

grammars.title: Plurals — and when you don't need one
after: **The ending ـها is always safe**, for things and people alike, in every situation. **ـان** is only for living beings and sounds more formal or literary. When in doubt, use ـها.
⚠️ **After a number, the noun stays singular**: سه کتاب ("three books", literally "three book"), not سه کتاب‌ها. This is exactly where English speakers trip — resist the urge to add a plural.
Persian also often **uses no plural at all** when the number doesn't matter: کتاب می‌خرم can mean "I'm buying books" — one or many, it doesn't matter, much like English "I'm buying bread".
Tehran speech shortens ـها to **ـا**: کتابا (*ketâbâ*), خونه‌ها (*khunehâ*), بچه‌ها (*bachehâ*).

blocks.text: Notice the pattern **ـخانه** ("house, place"), which builds the names of rooms and public places: آشپزخانه ("cook-house" = kitchen), کتابخانه ("book-house" = library), داروخانه ("medicine-house" = pharmacy), قهوه‌خانه ("coffee-house" = teahouse), چاپخانه ("print-house"). Like English *-house* in *greenhouse* or *lighthouse*: once you see خانه at the end of a word, you can almost always guess the meaning.

head: Talking to
Use
Why
rows: Even after knowing them a long time

blocks.text: The practical rule is simple: **when in doubt, use شما.** Using شما with a close friend only makes you sound stiff and polite; using تو with someone you don't know well sounds condescending. The second mistake costs far more than the first.

Persian also has a third, even more respectful level, used for elders and respected figures: **ایشان** (*ishân*) replaces او, and the verb goes into the plural. You don't need to use it yet, but you will hear it — and now you know it doesn't mean "they".

blocks.title: یخچال — a fridge older than electricity
items: The word یخچال is literally "ice pit" (یخ "ice" + چال "pit"). Before electricity, Iranians built huge mud-brick domes in the desert to store ice through the summer — some still stand in Yazd and Kerman today. When electric fridges arrived, they simply took the name.

Persian words are often built from honest, literal compounds like this: هواپیما ("air-measurer" = airplane), دستشویی ("hand-washing" = toilet), چشم‌پزشک ("eye doctor"). When you meet a long, unfamiliar word, try breaking it up first — the meaning often pops right out.

blocks.title: آقا and خانم — two words that are always safe
items: The words **آقا** (*âghâ*, "sir, Mr.") and **خانم** (*khânom*, "madam, Mrs./Ms.") are used far more often than "sir" and "madam" in English. They can stand alone to address a stranger (ببخشید آقا، ...) or go with a name: آقای احمدی، خانمِ رضایی.
⚠️ Notice that آقا becomes **آقای** (*âghâ-ye*) before a name, because of ezafe — while خانم becomes خانمِ. Both go **before** the family name, as in English.
There is a fridge in the kitchen.
There is no elevator here.
The book is on the table.
The wardrobe is next to the window.
There is nobody at home.
